title: THE PARABLE OF THE TEN VIRGINS IS MORE SOBERING THAN YOU REMEMBER
paragraphs: THE PARABLE OF THE TEN VIRGINS IS MORE SOBERING THAN YOU REMEMBER
The most frightening part of Matthew 25 is not that five women fell asleep. All ten did. The terrifying difference was revealed when somebody shouted in the darkness: “The bridegroom is coming.”
There is a sentence Jesus told His disciples that should make every person who calls himself or herself a Christian examine what is happening beneath the surface of their faith.
Not because Jesus wanted His followers terrified that He was unwilling to save them.
Not because salvation is earned by religious performance.
Not because one mistake can somehow overpower the blood of Christ.
But because it is possible to look ready for Jesus while living completely unprepared to meet Him.
That distinction is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Jesus said:
“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom.”
Ten virgins.
Ten lamps.
Ten people waiting for the same bridegroom.
Ten people who apparently expected him to come.
From a distance, there was almost nothing separating them.
And perhaps that is exactly why this parable is so disturbing.
Because Jesus did not describe five obvious enemies standing beside five faithful disciples.
He described ten people waiting.
Ten people carrying lamps.
Ten people who knew a bridegroom was coming.
Ten people who became tired.
Ten people who slept.
Ten people who eventually heard the announcement.
Yet only five entered the wedding feast.

If you have ever assumed that knowing Christian language, attending church, carrying a Bible, posting Scripture, listening to worship music, serving in ministry, growing up in a Christian family, or calling Jesus “Lord” automatically means your heart belongs to Him, do not rush past this parable.
Stay here.
Because before the story ends, a door closes.
And somebody standing outside that door is still saying,
“Lord, lord…”

Jesus tells this parable in Matthew 25:1–13, immediately following His teaching about His return and the necessity of watchfulness in Matthew 24. The context matters. This is not primarily a motivational story about being organized. It is an eschatological warning—a warning concerning readiness for the coming of the Son of Man.
The Greek opening is striking:
“Τότε ὁμοιωθήσεται ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν…”
“Then the kingdom of heaven will be compared to…”
Jesus places us inside a wedding scene.
The ten young women take their lamps and go out to meet the bridegroom. Five are described as wise and five as foolish.
The words are:
“πέντε δὲ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἦσαν μωραὶ καὶ πέντε φρόνιμοι.”
Five were μωραί—mōrai, foolish.
Five were φρόνιμοι—phronimoi, prudent, sensible, wise.
And immediately Jesus tells us what separated them.
The foolish took their lamps.
But they did not take oil with them.
The wise took oil in containers along with their lamps.
That sounds like such a small difference.
Until midnight.
That is often how spiritual neglect works.
It looks small before the crisis.
A prayer life slowly disappearing.
Secret sin quietly being protected.
Conviction repeatedly postponed.
Forgiveness continually resisted.
Repentance always scheduled for later.
Jesus publicly confessed but privately ignored.
A heart becoming colder while the Christian vocabulary remains intact.
Nobody necessarily notices.
The lamp is still there.
The appearance is still there.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
You still know the songs.
You can still quote verses.
You may even know exactly how to look spiritually alive.
But Jesus is not merely interested in whether you know how to carry a lamp.
He knows whether you belong to Him.
Then something happens in the parable that many people overlook.
The bridegroom delays.
Matthew writes:
“But while the bridegroom was delaying…”
And because he did not arrive when they expected, all ten became drowsy.
All ten slept.
Read that again.
The foolish slept.
But the wise slept too.
That matters because this parable is sometimes preached as though the wise virgins stayed awake all night while the foolish ones fell asleep.
That is not what Jesus said.
“ἐνύσταξαν πᾶσαι καὶ ἐκάθευδον.”
They all became drowsy and slept.
The decisive difference was not that one group possessed limitless physical stamina.
The difference was preparation.
The wise were ready for a delay.
Their readiness survived waiting.
And that speaks directly into a generation that has learned how to become excited about God but often struggles to endure with God.
It is one thing to cry during worship.
It is another thing to remain faithful when the emotion disappears.
It is one thing to promise Jesus everything after surviving a crisis.
It is another thing to walk with Him six months later when life feels ordinary again.
It is one thing to post, “God is good,” when the prayer is answered.
It is another thing to whisper, “Though He slay me, yet will I trust Him,” when heaven feels silent.
What happens to your faith when the Bridegroom seems delayed?
When you prayed and nothing changed?
When you obeyed and still suffered?
When somebody you loved died?
When the marriage did not heal the way you begged God to heal it?
When temptation came back?
When the excitement faded?
When you discovered that following Christ involves crosses as well as miracles?
That is where borrowed excitement stops being enough.
Midnight eventually comes.
And suddenly the silence is shattered.
“Ἰδοὺ ὁ νυμφίος, ἐξέρχεσθε εἰς ἀπάντησιν.”
“Behold, the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!”
Imagine that moment.
Eyes opening.
Feet hitting the ground.
Hands reaching for lamps.
Wicks being trimmed.
Hearts racing.
The waiting is over.
The bridegroom is here.
And suddenly something that had been invisible becomes painfully visible.
The foolish virgins realize their lamps are going out.
So they turn to the wise:
“Give us some of your oil.”
There is tragedy hidden inside that request.
Because there are things another Christian can share with you.
Someone can share Scripture with you.
Someone can preach to you.
Someone can pray for you.
Someone can disciple you.
Someone can encourage you.
Someone can tell you about Jesus.
Someone can sit beside your hospital bed and remind you of eternity.
Your grandmother can pray for you for thirty years.
Your pastor can preach Christ until his voice gives out.
Your spouse can plead with you to come home to God.
Your mother can put your name on every prayer list she can find.
Your friend can send you this article tonight.
But nobody can repent for you.
Nobody can believe in Christ for you.
Nobody can surrender your heart for you.
Nobody can have your relationship with Jesus on your behalf.
Christian parents cannot transfer salvation genetically.
A church cannot place Christ into an unrepentant heart through proximity.
And one believer's faithfulness cannot substitute for another person's unbelief.
There comes a point when borrowed Christianity is exposed.
This does not mean Christians should refuse to help others. Scripture repeatedly commands love, generosity, intercession, discipleship, correction, encouragement, and the proclamation of the Gospel.
The point is different.
There are realities of personal allegiance to Christ that cannot be transferred at the final moment.
And we should be careful here with the oil.

Throughout Christian history, interpreters have suggested various meanings for the oil. Some associate it with the Holy Spirit, others with genuine faith, persevering obedience, spiritual readiness, or the inward reality accompanying outward profession.
But Jesus does not explicitly stop the parable and say, “The oil represents this one specific thing.”
So we should not pretend He did.
The unmistakable emphasis is readiness.
Five were prepared for the bridegroom.
Five were not.
And when the bridegroom finally arrived, there was no longer time to manufacture yesterday's preparation.
While the foolish virgins went away to obtain oil, the bridegroom came.
Then Scripture says:
“καὶ αἱ ἕτοιμοι εἰσῆλθον μετ’ αὐτοῦ εἰς τοὺς γάμους…”
“And those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast.”
Those who were ready entered.
And then come five Greek words carrying enormous weight:
“καὶ ἐκλείσθη ἡ θύρα.”
“And the door was shut.”
The door.
Was.
Shut.
There are moments in Scripture when a short sentence feels heavier than an entire chapter.
This is one of them.
Because the Bible's message of grace is gloriously open.
Christ receives sinners.
Jesus ate with people respectable religion despised.
He touched the unclean.
He welcomed the broken.
He forgave the guilty.
He restored failures.
He told weary sinners to come.
The Gospel invitation goes into the world.
“Come.”
“Believe.”
“Repent.”
“Receive.”
Christ's mercy is greater than the scandal of your past.
But the Bible never teaches that the opportunity to repent should therefore be treated casually forever.
Grace is not permission to postpone Christ.
Grace is the reason to run to Him now.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 6:2:
There is an urgency to the Gospel precisely because eternity is real.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been postponing Jesus for years.
“Later.”
When I am older.
When I finish enjoying myself.
When I fix my life.
When I stop this addiction.
When I get married.
When the children grow up.
When business slows down.
When I have fewer problems.
When I finally feel spiritual.
Later.
Later.
Later.
But you were never promised later.
You were given today.
And Christianity is not ultimately about cleaning yourself enough to approach Jesus.
If you could save yourself, Calvary would have been unnecessary.
The Gospel says something far more astonishing.
You cannot make yourself righteous before God, so the righteous Son of God came for sinners.
Jesus lived the obedience we failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
Your hope is not that you can accumulate enough religious oil to purchase heaven.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not the achievement of human boasting.
But saving grace does not leave a person permanently indifferent to the Savior.
Grace transforms.
Faith bears fruit.
The forgiven begin learning obedience.
The redeemed begin longing for the Redeemer.
Not perfectly.
Not without stumbling.
Not without battles.
But genuinely.
That is why this parable should not drive a sincere struggling Christian into obsessive terror every time they fail.
Peter failed spectacularly.
He denied Jesus three times.
And Jesus restored him.
Thomas doubted.
Jesus met him.
The disciples fled.
Christ gathered them again.
The Christian Gospel is not “Never stumble or Jesus will stop loving you.”
The Gospel is that sinners are saved by the grace of God through Christ—and those who belong to Christ are called to abide in Him, trust Him, follow Him, repent when they sin, and persevere in faith.
There is a difference between struggling with sin and making peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and deciding you no longer want to get up.
There is a difference between weakness that cries, “Jesus, help me,” and rebellion that says, “Jesus, leave me alone.”
Maybe you are tired.
Maybe your prayer life is barely a whisper.
Maybe you have been fighting the same temptation so long that you are embarrassed to tell anyone.
Maybe you opened this article feeling like a hypocrite.
Maybe nobody knows what happened last night.
Maybe everybody thinks your marriage is fine.
Maybe your children think your faith is strong.
Maybe your church friends see the smile but never see you crying in the car before walking through the doors.
Maybe your Bible has stayed closed longer than you want to admit.
Maybe you love Jesus, but your spirit feels exhausted.
Then hear this carefully:
The answer is not pretending harder.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
Return to Christ.

First John 1:9 does not tell believers to hide their sin until they become impressive enough for God. It says that if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
There is cleansing for the person willing to stop hiding.
There is grace for the ashamed.
There is restoration for the fallen.
There is forgiveness for sinners.
There is a cross standing between your guilt and God's judgment.
And there is an empty tomb declaring that sin and death do not get the final word over those who are in Christ.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter's scandal did not become the final chapter.
The cross was not the end of the story.
Your worst chapter does not possess authority to write your ending when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of your life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But then Jesus brings the parable back to its terrifying conclusion.
The foolish virgins return.
The door has already closed.
And they cry:
“Κύριε κύριε, ἄνοιξον ἡμῖν.”
“Lord, lord, open to us.”
Notice what they call Him.
Lord.
That should sober every churchgoing person reading this.
Religious vocabulary alone is not saving faith.
Knowing what to call Jesus is not the same as belonging to Jesus.

The language also echoes another terrifying warning from Christ in Matthew 7:21–23, where people say, “Lord, Lord,” while Jesus exposes the absence of a genuine relationship expressed in obedience to the Father's will.
Then comes the answer nobody wants to imagine hearing:
“Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς.”
“Truly I say to you, I do not know you.”
Not:
“You did not collect enough achievements.”
Not:
“You were not famous enough.”
Not:
“You did not have enough followers.”
Not:
“You weren't successful enough.”
“I do not know you.”
Christianity reaches its center here.
Jesus.
Not merely information about Jesus.
Not Christian aesthetics.
Not denominational identity.
Not inherited religion.
Not public performance.
Jesus Christ Himself.
This is why eternal life is described relationally in John 17:3: knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent.
And this is why the question underneath the parable is far more personal than:
“Do you believe the Second Coming is real?”
The deeper question is:
Do you know the Bridegroom?
And does He know you as His own?
Then Jesus gives the command that should follow us long after we finish reading:
“Γρηγορεῖτε οὖν…”
Grēgoreite oun.
“Therefore, keep watch.”
“For you know neither the day nor the hour.”
Watch.
Not by staring nervously at the sky every morning.
Not by setting dates Jesus told us we do not know.
Not by turning every headline into speculative prophecy.
Watch by belonging faithfully to Christ.
Watch by refusing to make peace with hidden sin.
Watch by forgiving.
Watch by praying.
Watch by remaining in His Word.
Watch by loving your neighbor.
Watch by carrying the Gospel.
Watch by remembering that your possessions will stay here.
Your trophies will stay here.
Your titles will stay here.
Your house will belong to somebody else.
Your phone will eventually stop ringing.
Your social-media account will eventually become silent.
And one day somebody may speak about you in the past tense.
But Christ will still be King.
So what are you waiting for?
If you need to repent, repent now.
If you need to forgive, begin now.
If you need to confess something hidden, bring it into the light.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have never trusted Jesus Christ, stop treating eternity like an appointment you are guaranteed the opportunity to reschedule.
Come to Christ.
Not because you have become worthy.
Come because He is merciful.
Come because the cross is enough.
Come because the tomb is empty.
Come because the Bridegroom is worth knowing.
And if your heart is saying, “But you don't know what I've done…”
No.
I may not.
Jesus does.
The woman caught in sin had a scandal.
The thief beside Christ had a scandal.
Peter had a scandal.
Paul carried memories of persecuting the church.
The Bible is filled with people whose histories would have destroyed their reputations.
Then grace entered the story.
Grace did not rename evil as good.
Grace confronted sin, forgave sinners who came to God through faith, and created new lives.
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Not scandal to excuses.
Not scandal to religious camouflage.
Scandal to repentance.
Scandal to the cross.
Scandal to forgiveness.
Scandal to transformation.
Scandal to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe somebody came to your mind while you were reading.
Send it to them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not as a weapon.
Send it because you love them enough to want them at the wedding feast.
You do not know where this message will land.
If your spirit has been exhausted lately, comment, “pray for me.”
If you have been fighting to remain faithful, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If Christ is exposing something you have been hiding, comment, “no more hiding.”
If you know God is still restoring your life, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And if this brought you face-to-face with your need for mercy, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Not because typing words into a comment box saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building around ourselves.
And read the other comments.
Pray for somebody.
Encourage somebody.
Remind somebody that repentance is not the end of hope.
It is where the sinner stops running from the One who can save.
There may come a night when you need to read Matthew 25 again.
There may come a season when your lamp feels dim and waiting feels unbearably long.
Return to Jesus' words.
The Bridegroom may seem delayed.
But the Bridegroom has not forgotten His promise.
It does not purchase salvation, blessing, answered prayer, or a better standing before Christ. The Gospel cannot be bought.
But supporting Gospel work can be an act of Christian generosity when it is done freely, joyfully, and for the glory of God.
But the greatest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is Jesus.

If this ministry continually turns your attention toward Christ, strengthens you in Scripture, challenges hidden compromise, encourages you when faith becomes difficult, and equips you to help another person find the Gospel, then consider becoming part of what keeps that work moving.
And whether or not you are able to support financially, you can still help carry the Gospel farther.
Pray for the people reading beside you.
And above everything else, follow Jesus.
Because eventually every lamp, every reputation, every religious appearance, every excuse, and every hidden chamber of the heart will encounter the same announcement:
The Bridegroom has come.
And when that moment arrives, you will not care how many people thought you looked Christian.
You will care about one thing.
Jesus.
So do not merely admire the lamp.
Know the Bridegroom.
Do not merely prepare your public image.
Bring Him your heart.
Do not wait until the door closes to become serious about the One standing on the other side.
Come while mercy is calling.
Come while grace is being offered.
Come with the addiction.
Come with the shame.
Come with the questions.
Come with the secret.
Come with the years you wasted.
Come with the failure you cannot undo.
Come with empty hands.
Come to the cross.
And discover that the Savior who warns us so seriously about the closed door is the same Savior who stretched His arms open on a cross to bring sinners home.
Perhaps that is the sentence worth carrying with you tonight:
Do not wait until midnight to discover that you spent your whole life carrying the lamp while never truly knowing the Bridegroom.
